headline: On an endless grid, the first player can always build the six-square Snaky shape within 21 moves.
scope: The game starts on an empty infinite square grid, Maker moves first, and turned or flipped copies of Snaky count.
plain: Two players take turns claiming squares of an endless grid. Maker wants six squares forming the Snaky shape; Breaker only blocks. Whether Maker can win on a flat board without a head start was long undecided. This paper proves Maker wins within 21 of its own moves.
doesNot: This does not show that 21 moves is the fewest possible, and it says nothing about the game where both players race for Snaky.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles a long-open case of polyomino achievement games, with a checked strategy.

explanation:
Draw a row of four squares on graph paper. Step up one square from the last, then add one more square to the right. That six-square shape is called Snaky. It can be turned and flipped. Counting carefully, there are eight different versions of it on the grid.

Now play a game on an endless grid. Two players, Maker and Breaker, take turns claiming one empty square each. Maker goes first[3]. Maker wins by owning all six squares of some copy of Snaky, in any of its turned or flipped forms[1,2]. Breaker only tries to stop Maker. Breaker does not need a shape of its own. This is called a Maker–Breaker game.

Earlier work settled Snaky only in other settings. Sieben showed in 2004 that Maker wins in 41 dimensions[8]. Halupczok and Schlage-Puchta showed in 2007 that Maker wins in three dimensions, but loses on an 8 by 8 board[9]. They also showed Maker wins in the plane with a handicap of one. That means Maker places two squares on its first turn[10]. In 2008, Sieben described the ordinary flat game as undecided[11].

This paper proves that Maker wins on the empty flat grid, with no handicap. Maker can always complete Snaky within 21 of its own moves[4]. Breaker may play anywhere, by any legal rule. In whole turns, Maker wins by the 41st turn of the game[5]. The paper says the same bound holds on a finite 17 by 17 board[6]. It does not claim that 21 is the fewest moves possible[7].

The difficulty is that the board never ends. Breaker can play far away, or right next to Maker's squares. A computer cannot search every game on an endless board. The paper turns the strategy into a finite record, called a certificate. It lists 728 numbered winning positions, each built from simpler ones[12]. Each position names squares Maker must own, a region Breaker must avoid, and a move budget. The final position needs no Maker squares, a region of 251 squares, and 21 moves[13].

The key step is simple to state. Maker claims a square that keeps several winning plans alive at once. Breaker's next single square cannot block all of them[14]. So at least one plan always survives. Squares Breaker claims outside the region do not matter.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the main claim. The Lean scope note says it gives a legal strategy that wins within 21 Maker moves on the endless board. It checks against every legal Breaker play. The smaller finite-board statement is outside that check. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid. Lean has checked the 21-move strategy on the endless board; the finite-board claim is outside the check, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A six-square shape: a row of four squares, then a step up and one more square.
A game where one player tries to build a shape and the other only tries to block it.
A shape made of squares joined edge to edge.
Extra squares given to Maker at the start; a handicap of one means two squares on the first turn.
A finite list of positions and moves that records a full winning strategy.
